Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: -1 means 'not reached yet'; it doubles as the visited marker
Combine distance and visited in one grid
seed `q` with EVERY 0 cell at distance 0
Multi-source BFS (Breadth-First Search): all zeros start together
The nearest 0 for each cell is the shortest path from ANY zero
Process cells in order of distance
FIFO (First In, First Out) order makes the first time a cell is reached the shortest
A neighbour is one step farther than the cell that reached it

p: `[[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[1,1,1]]`. The five zeros seed the queue at distance 0; each BFS wave labels the cells one step farther.
The final grid is `[[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[1,2,1]]`: the bottom-middle cell is 2 away from the nearest zero.

blocks.h: Why start from the zeros rather than from every 1?
p: BFS from each `1` costs O((mn)²) in total. One BFS seeded with all zeros computes every distance in a single O(mn) sweep, because 'distance to the nearest zero' is exactly the BFS depth in the combined search.

bullets: Time: O(m·n), each cell is queued once.

542.takeaway: Distance to the nearest 0: multi-source BFS seeded with all zeros; the first time a cell is reached is its shortest distance.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Leaves are handled separately so they are never counted twice
The root starts the boundary; a lone root is a leaf and will be added by the leaf pass
Walk down preferring `left`, else `right`, skipping leaves
The boundary goes down the left edge, and turns right only when there is no left child
Pre-order DFS (Depth-First Search) collecting leaves left to right
Walk down preferring `right`, else `left`, skipping leaves
Reverse so the right boundary is emitted bottom to top (counter-clockwise)

p: Tree `1` with right child `2` whose children are `3` and `4`:

The boundary is: left edge (top to bottom), then all leaves (left to right), then right edge (bottom to top). Doing them separately keeps each rule simple, and excluding leaves from the edge walks guarantees every node appears once. Without the leaf exclusion the bottom-most boundary nodes would appear twice.

On the left boundary, if a node has no left child the walk switches to the right child (`node.left if node.left else node.right`). The same mirror rule applies on the right. `[1,null,2,3,4]` has no left boundary at all, but the right boundary is `2` (then the leaf `4` is skipped).

bullets: Time: O(n), each pass visits each node at most once.
Space: O(h) recursion plus the output.

545.takeaway: Tree boundary = root, left edge without leaves, all leaves, right edge without leaves reversed.

Edge position counts: {1: 3, 2: 1, 3: 3, 4: 4, 5: 2}. Position 4 appears in 4 rows, so a line there crosses 6 - 4 = 2 rows. The answer is 2.

rows: One entry per list: its current element, which list, and the index in it
Largest of the current elements: the right end of the current window
The heap gives the left end (min); `hi` tracks the max separately
Contains one element from each list by construction
The smallest range covering all lists
Advance the list that currently supplies the smallest value, the only move that can shrink the range

p: Lists `[4,10,15,24,26]`, `[0,9,12,20]`, `[5,18,22,30]`. Each row pops the current minimum and pushes the next element of the same list.

The window always holds one element per list. To make the range smaller, either the minimum must rise or the maximum must fall. The maximum can't fall (each list element is only replaced by a larger one), so the only way to improve is to move the minimum forward. Moving any other element only increases `hi` or leaves the range the same.

Time

bullets: Time: O(N log k), N total elements and k lists.

632.takeaway: Smallest range covering k lists: min-heap of one element per list, track the max, and repeatedly advance the list that holds the minimum.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: List of `(id, timestamp)` in arrival order
Granularity → how many characters of the fixed-width timestamp to compare
The format `YYYY:MM:DD:HH:MM:SS` is fixed-width, so a prefix is a time unit
The timestamp truncated to the chosen unit
String comparison works because the fields are zero-padded and ordered most significant first

p: Year granularity returns `[1, 2, 3]`; Hour granularity returns `[1, 2]`, since log 3 (`2016:01:01:00`) is before the start hour `2016:01:01:01`.

Fixed-width, zero-padded fields mean the first differing character decides the order, and that character is in the most significant differing unit. So comparing truncated prefixes equals comparing the times at that granularity.

635.takeaway: Log storage: fixed-width timestamps compare correctly as strings, so truncating to the granularity prefix gives range queries by unit.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Minimum cost to buy exactly the quantities in the tuple `need`
Lists aren't hashable; tuples are, so they can be cache keys
Cost with no offers: buy everything at the regular price
The quantities in an offer; the last element is its price
The offer must not exceed what is still needed
Use the offer once, then solve the remainder
Overlapping subproblems (different offer orders reach the same remainder)

p: Prices `[2,5]`, offers `[3,0,5]` and `[1,2,10]`, needs `[3,2]`. States are solved depth-first; each row is a state solved for the first time:

`go((3, 2))` is 14: apply the offer `[1,2,10]` once (10), leaving need `(2, 0)`, which costs 2 × 2 = 4 at list price. The other offer `[3,0,5]` leaves need `(0, 2)`, which costs 10, for a total of 15, and buying everything at list price costs 16.
Using offer A then offer B reaches the same remainder as B then A. Without the cache the search re-solves these orders; with it each distinct `need` tuple is solved once.

638.takeaway: Shopping offers: memoised recursion on the tuple of remaining needs; at each state try buying the rest at list price or applying any offer that does not overbuy.

The first free slot after the last element, wrapping around

p: Capacity 3. `a` is the raw array, `head` the front index:

blocks.h: Why track `size` instead of head and tail?
p: With only two indices, an empty buffer and a full buffer both look like `head == tail`. A separate `size` removes that ambiguity without wasting a slot. The rear is derived: `head + size - 1`.

When the front moves left from index 0 it must land at the last index, and when the rear passes the end it must wrap to 0. The modulo gives that wrap-around in one expression; every operation is O(1).

641.takeaway: Circular deque on a fixed array: keep `head` and `size`, and wrap every index with `% capacity`.

Expand outward while the ends match; every success is one more palindromic substring

Counting by position, not by distinct text

p: `s = "aaa"` has 5 centers and 6 palindromic substrings (`a`, `a`, `a`, `aa`, `aa`, `aaa`):

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Candidate prime factor, tried in increasing order
A factor `d` costs `d` operations: one Copy All plus `d - 1` Pastes
Cost of multiplying the screen by `d`
Reduce what is left to build

p: `n = 12 = 2 · 2 · 3`: the answer is the SUM of the prime factors.

blocks.h: Why is the answer the sum of prime factors?
p: To go from `k` characters to `k·d` you copy once and paste `d - 1` times: `d` operations. Building `n` is a chain of such multiplications, so the cost is the sum of the factors used. Splitting a composite `a·b` into `a` then `b` costs `a + b`, which is never more than `a·b` for `a, b ≥ 2`, so using primes is optimal.

blocks.h: Why no divisibility check for prime `d`?
p: Because small factors were already divided out, any `d` that divides `n` at this point is prime. A composite `d` can't divide a remaining `n` whose smaller prime factors are gone.

bullets: Time: O(n) worst case (when n is prime, `d` counts up to n); O(√n) with a stop at √n and handling the leftover prime.

650.takeaway: 2 Keys Keyboard = sum of the prime factors of n, found by trial division.

p: The set solution ignores the ordering and works on any binary tree, in O(n) time and O(n) space. Using the BST (in-order list plus two pointers, or BST iterators from both ends) gives O(n) time with O(h) space for the iterator version.

653.takeaway: Two Sum on a BST: a hash set of seen values during any traversal; the BST property enables an O(h)-space two-iterator variant.

Meaning

rows: Each node carries its position index as if the tree were a complete binary tree
Heap-style numbering: children of `i` are `2i` and `2i + 1`
Index of the leftmost node of the level
Shift indices so each level starts at 0, which keeps numbers small
Prevents huge integers on deep, skewed trees (in fixed-width languages it prevents overflow)
Index of the rightmost node after the loop (the final one popped)
Width counts the empty slots between the end nodes too
The problem defines width by end nodes, nulls included

p: `[1,3,2,5,3,null,9]`. Each row lists `(value, normalised index)` for one level:

blocks.h: Why indexes instead of counting nodes?
p: Null children between two real nodes still count toward width. Giving every node the index it would have in a complete tree turns width into a simple subtraction: rightmost minus leftmost plus one.

Without normalising, an index at depth d can reach 2^d. Subtracting the leftmost index per level keeps values bounded by the level's width. In Python integers don't overflow, but in Java/C++ this is an essential detail.

662.takeaway: Maximum width: BFS (Breadth-First Search) with heap-style indices (children 2i and 2i+1), normalised per level; width = rightmost − leftmost + 1.

p: `[2,2,5,null,null,5,7]`: the root and its left child are 2 (the minimum), the right child 5 is the first larger value.

blocks.h: Why can we stop at the first larger value on each path?
p: In this special tree a parent is the minimum of its two children (each node's value equals the smaller child). So every descendant of a node with value `v` is at least `v`. The first value above `first` on a path is therefore the smallest on that path, and descending further only finds larger ones.

p: If every node equals the root there is no second minimum and `res` stays `-1`.

671.takeaway: Second minimum in a 'parent = min of children' tree: the root is the minimum, so search only through nodes equal to it and stop at the first larger value.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Ceiling division using floor division of a negative: `ceil(x / y) = -(-x // y)`
The minimum copies needed just to be long enough to contain `b`
Only these two repetition counts can work
`b` can start anywhere inside the first copy, costing at most one extra copy
Substring test on the repeated string
Python's `in` is a fast substring search
If neither works, no number of repeats ever will

p: `a = "abcd"`, `b = "cdabcdab"` (length 8, so `times = 2`):

`b` starts at some offset `o < len(a)` in the repeated string, so it spans from `o` to `o + len(b)`. The needed length is at most `len(a) - 1 + len(b)`, i.e. `ceil(len(b)/len(a)) + 1` copies. Beyond that, more copies add nothing new because the pattern is periodic. Fewer than `times` copies are shorter than `b`.

head: Copies
Why
rows: works if b aligns with the start of a copy

bullets: Time: O(len(a) + len(b)) with an efficient substring search; Python's `in` is fast in practice but O(n·m) in the worst case.
Space: O(len(a) + len(b)) for the repeated string.

686.takeaway: Repeated string match: only ceil(|b|/|a|) and one more repetition need testing, using a substring check.
